summary: Radar for 2026-10-31, GLP-1 focus. The retatrutide vs semaglutide head-to-head (Oct 28) has peaked: TV networks and trade press have all covered it. The one useful angle left is a Short on "more people quit over side effects". Orforglipron ATTAIN-J (Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol, Oct 30) is the only fresh randomized result. I checked it: 238 Japanese adults, −5.9% / −8.7% / −7.9% vs −0.6% placebo at 72 weeks. That's modest, the population is narrow, and results were already posted on the trial registry before the paper, so it doesn't meet the 48-hour Lane C test. It goes to a 13:00 Short, not a long-form. No qualifying Lane C news today, so Lane A runs as the playbook says. Two new seasonal hooks came up with early pickup: cold and flu season on tirzepatide (Yahoo Health, Oct 31) and telling your dentist or anaesthetist before sedation (Yahoo Health, Oct 31). Both are caution-rated: we explain the 'why' and the 'tell your clinician', with no hold or stop advice. Fatigue got fresh consumer coverage (Oct 30), and a hydration-linked kidney stone cohort (J Clin Med) supports the planned 'fatigue and hydration' Lane A slot. Thanksgiving is the strongest seasonal long-form: it has appeared in 6 snapshots with steady momentum, and peak search is Nov 15–27. A new DOM study on how grocery purchases change on GLP-1 treatment (Oct 29) and McDonald's GLP-1 menu news give it a fresh hook. ObesityWeek (Nov 14–17, Washington DC) is the next catalyst for Lane C, so watch it for full retatrutide, CagriSema and tirzepatide data. Rejected: online program and 'where to buy' affiliate lists (Fortune, Forbes, Page Six, Woman's World), research-vial retatrutide pricing, compounded-with-B12 promotion, and the cost and employer-coverage stories (banned lanes). The eating-disorder restriction story (Psychiatric Times) is left out because of brand guardrails.

candidates.topic: What happens when you stop tirzepatide? SURMOUNT-4 (783 began the lead-in; 335 vs 335 randomized at week 36; +14.0% regain from week 36 to 88 on placebo) plus the Metabolites systematic review of regain after GLP-1 and GIP/GLP-1 medicines (Oct 9)
candidates.angle: Lane A long-form, next in the queue. Open on 'you're wondering what happens if you ever come off it' and answer in the first sentence: on average, weight comes back when the medicine stops, and people who stayed on it kept losing. Then cover what the trials show about who keeps more off, and why habits built now (protein, strength, routines) matter. Say 'don't stop or change your medicines on your own' and 'talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you'.

candidates.topic: Orforglipron ATTAIN-J, peer-reviewed in Lancet Diabetes Endocrinol (Oct 30): 238 Japanese adults with obesity disease, 72 weeks; weight −5.9% (6 mg), −8.7% (12 mg), −7.9% (36 mg) vs −0.6% placebo
candidates.angle: 13:00 'what's confirmed?' Short on the GLP-1 pill. Make clear this is a Japanese population with smaller average losses than the global trials, and why populations differ (separate trials, not head-to-head). Nausea and vomiting caused most of the discontinuations. Not Lane C: the results were posted on the trial registry before the paper, and orforglipron already has a long-form.
candidates.why_now: Published Oct 30 with almost no consumer coverage yet. Orforglipron is a drug people search for (our long-form earned 202 min).
